kernelIdea: V is inductive if 0 ∈ V and x ∈ V ⇒ S(x) ∈ V. Axiom 9 says every inductive set contains ℕ, ruling out models with extra elements and giving ℕ = {0,1,2,…} exactly.

kernels.l1: Nothing but the counting numbers gets in.
kernels.l2: If a box has zero in it, and always has the next one whenever it has a number, then that box has every counting number in it. Nothing extra is allowed to sneak in.
kernels.l3: A set is inductive if it contains 0 and always contains the next of anything in it. The last axiom says the counting numbers sit inside every inductive set — which is what stops extra strangers joining the counting numbers.
kernels.l4: V is inductive if 0 ∈ V and x ∈ V ⇒ S(x) ∈ V. Axiom 9 says every inductive set contains ℕ. This excludes models with extra elements and, with Axioms 1–8, pins ℕ down to exactly {0, 1, 2, …}.
kernels.l5: Axiom 9 is mathematical induction: 0 ∈ V is the base case and closure under S is the inductive step.
kernels.l6: The final set equality ℕ = {0,1,2,…} is obtained by double inclusion, with Axiom 9 supplying one direction and Axioms 5–6 the other.
kernels.l7: Axiom 9 states that every inductive set contains ℕ; it is mathematical induction in set form, it excludes models with rogue elements, and with the earlier axioms it determines ℕ up to isomorphism.
kernels.l8: Second-order Peano arithmetic determines ℕ up to isomorphism; the first-order induction schema does not, and the resulting nonstandard models are the subject of model theory.

kernel: V is inductive if 0 ∈ V and x ∈ V ⇒ S(x) ∈ V. Axiom 9: if V is inductive then ℕ ⊆ V. This rules out "too big" models and, combined with axioms 1–8, gives ℕ = {0,1,2,…} exactly. It is the same principle as Chapter 6.
